miner_guide.text: Hard hat on? Good. Lamp on? Better. Spare lamp? Best. Mind the drip. It's Atlantic, and it's cold.

miner_old.text: I worked here from 1969. They'd turn the lights out for the knockers' sake. I swear I heard them.
The seams ran out under the sea. You could hear the boulders rolling in a storm. A lot of men were braver than me.

miner_kid.text: The tin goes into bronze, and solder, and tin cans. Cornish tin was traded to the Phoenicians, they say, in ancient days.
I'm doing work experience. My job is to hold the torch. I hold it well.

then.text: I'm going home to Bath. To soak. Alone. With a flask. Do not post anything.

else.text: The deepest chamber of Geevor: a low gallery, tin-bright in the lamplight, humming with a patient, knocking sound. Sir Rupert stands at the centre with a briefcase and a hard hat that doesn't suit him.
The knockers! The little tin spirits. You can hear them, can't you? Knock, knock, knock. Valuable, utterly valuable. I plan to put them in a display case.
A faint, offended knock answers from the wall. It sounds like a hundred small miners clearing their throats at once.
Hush. They'll sign. I've got a form. It's got a tick box for 'knocking'.
Down here again? This is a hard-hat area. Have you a hard hat? No? Then this is a battle area.
The knocking stops. Then, very politely, it starts again: a single knock, slow and steady, like a round of applause.
Lord Vane will hear of this. He hears of everything, eventually, usually over breakfast.
Ashcombe stuffs his form into his briefcase and hurries up the adit. The Wardens trail after him, looking mildly relieved.
Meur ras, my lover. That's 'thank you' in Cornish. The knockers don't say it themselves, but they mean it.
Your phone buzzes. The signal in a tin mine is surprisingly good. Professor Garside sounds as if she is standing in a kitchen.
{player}! I felt that one in my fillings. Sir Rupert is down. Marvellous. You're a credit to Macclesfield and a nuisance to the Enclosure.
Now, Ireland. The stones across the water are humming in a way I can only describe as lyrical. I'm sending you a ferry ticket. It's in your bag. I printed it. I laminated it.
The ferry leaves from Holyhead. Take the rail to Llanberis, then walk west over the Menai Bridge and across Anglesey. The sailor will want to see that ticket.
And bring a coat. The Irish Sea has opinions.
A faint, warm knock follows you out of the mine, like a send-off.

gate_geevor.text: Deep end's closed. Sir Rupert's orders. He likes to meet people properly, up at Tintagel, before they come down a mine.
He's very particular. He once made me re-introduce myself to my own boots.
